excerpt_integrity_check.method: Mechanically checked each evidence text as an exact contiguous substring of summary-snapshot.md.
excerpt_integrity_check.complete_unit_selection_check: Each evidence text is a complete paragraph, complete bullet-list unit, or complete consecutive numbered list items; headings identify the source subsection. No tables were used.

clauses: Alien selection procedure for a three-player standard game.
Which flares enter the cosmic deck.
Cards dealt to each player.
First-player selection.
answers.answer: Each player is dealt two flares and the matching alien sheets, secretly chooses one alien, and returns the other sheet. Add both dealt flares for every player, including rejected aliens’ flares, to the cosmic deck; add random extras if needed to reach ten total. Deal eight cards to each player. Draw destiny until a player color appears; that player starts, then shuffle the drawn card back into the destiny deck.

evidence.heading: Setup
evidence.text:
1. Put the warp in the center. Each player takes five planets of one color, places four of their twenty ships on each, and places their colony marker beside the warp's 0 space.
2. Remove destiny cards naming unused player colors; shuffle the rest, including wilds and specials.
3. Shuffle the flares, deal two to each player, and give them the matching alien sheets. Each secretly chooses one alien, initially placing it facedown, and returns the other sheet to the box. This is the standard selection procedure; Hidden Powers is a separate excluded variant. The original text does not specify when standard-game sheets are turned faceup; unlike the optional Hidden Powers rule, it gives no explicit reveal window. This source gap is recorded rather than supplying a new setup rule. Green/yellow/red indicate recommended experience, not strength. Beginners may start with green aliens without flares.
4. Add **both flares dealt to every player**, including rejected aliens' flares, to the cosmic deck. Add random extras if needed to reach ten flares total; shuffle. Deal eight-card hands. Keep card faces private unless an effect allows showing them.
5. Draw destiny until a player color appears; that player starts. Shuffle the drawn card back into the destiny deck. Play passes left thereafter.

clauses: What counts as one colony.
Whether several players can have colonies on one planet.
Whether five foreign colonies must be in different systems.
answers.answer: A colony is one or more ships of one color on one planet; several colors can each have their own colony on the same planet. Five foreign colonies may all be in one other system.

evidence.heading: Overview
evidence.text: Each player leads an alien trying to establish five **foreign colonies**. A colony is one or more ships of one color on one planet; extra ships on that planet do not make extra colonies. Several colors can coexist there, each with its own colony. Home colonies are in your own system; foreign colonies are outside it. Five foreign planets can all be in one other system. Alien powers override conflicting general rules.

clauses: Whether offense must retrieve a warp ship when available at encounter start.
Where the original rulebook places it when offense has colonies or has none.
answers.answer: Yes. If offense has a colony, place the ship on any existing home or foreign colony. If offense has no colonies, the original rulebook places it directly in the gate. The FAQ adds that a player with no colonies or ships on their turn may instead place it on any home planet.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 1. Regroup
evidence.text: Offense must retrieve one of its ships from the warp if available, placing it on any existing home or foreign colony. The original rulebook puts this retrieved ship directly in the gate if offense has no colonies. The FAQ adds that a player who has no colonies or ships on their turn may instead place the Regroup ship on any home planet. Ordinary relocation with no colony to receive ships sends them to the warp; the stated Regroup exceptions take precedence.

clauses: What happens when only one destiny card remains.
Choices when own color is drawn and the home system contains a foreign colony.
Choice when own color is drawn and there is a completely empty home planet.
answers.answer: When one destiny card remains, shuffle it with the destiny discards before drawing from the new deck. On own color, offense may redraw or target one chosen foreign colony in its home system, making its owner the defense; other colonies there are bystanders. Alternatively, offense can target a home planet with no ships of any color, move up to four ships from other colonies there, and reclaim it automatically; this counts as a win and successful encounter.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 2. Destiny
evidence.text: Draw destiny to determine the defense and target system. **When only one card remains, do not draw it**: shuffle it with the destiny discards, then draw from the new deck.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 2. Destiny
evidence.text:
- Another player's color: encounter that player in their home system.
- Your own color: redraw, or target one chosen foreign colony in your home system, making its owner the defense. Other colonies there are bystanders. You can instead aim at a home planet with **no ships of any color**, moving up to four ships from other colonies there to reclaim it automatically. This counts as a win and successful encounter, proceeds only through Launch, and can qualify you for a second encounter.
- Wild: choose another player and encounter them in their home system.
- Special: follow its conditions, defense and location. For color-dependent effects such as Shadow, treat it as the designated defense's color.

clauses: Whether drawing Blue permits attacking Blue’s foreign colony in Red’s home system without a special power.
Who defends Red’s empty home planet when foreign bystanders are present.
answers.answer: No. Blue destiny targets Blue in Blue’s home system; ordinary rules do not permit attacking a foreign colony in a third player’s system. Red, as home-system owner, defends Red’s empty home planet even with zero ships; other colors’ colonies are bystanders and do not add to defense or suffer the result.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 2. Destiny
evidence.text: Destiny hazard symbols have no effect in this base game. Ordinarily you cannot attack a player's foreign colony in a third player's system: a color/wild/special targets its defense in that player's home system, while your own color permits driving out a foreign colony in your own system. If you already have colonies on **all planets in the defensive system**, draw destiny again.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 3. Launch
evidence.text: Defense cannot add or subtract ships on the target. The owner of a home system defends their planet even with zero ships there. Other colors' colonies are **bystanders**: they add nothing to the defense and the encounter result does not harm them. When driving out a foreign colony, target only that one color's colony; all other colors are bystanders.

clauses: Launch ship source and quantity.
Whether offense may strip a colony.
Whether defense may move ships onto or off the target during Launch.
answers.answer: Offense launches one to four ships from any combination of existing home and foreign colonies and may strip a colony; removing its last ship immediately eliminates it. Defense cannot add or subtract ships on the target during Launch.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 3. Launch
evidence.text: Aim the gate at one planet in the indicated system; put one to four of your ships in it, drawn from any combination of your existing home and foreign colonies. You may strip a colony, but removing its last ship immediately eliminates it. Ships returning from an encounter or warp cannot return to that now-empty location as though it remained your colony.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 3. Launch
evidence.text: Defense cannot add or subtract ships on the target. The owner of a home system defends their planet even with zero ships there. Other colors' colonies are **bystanders**: they add nothing to the defense and the encounter result does not harm them. When driving out a foreign colony, target only that one color's colony; all other colors are bystanders.

clauses: Order of invitations and commitments.
Whether a player invited by both sides may join both.
Where defensive allies put their ships.
answers.answer: Offense invites first and invitees wait; defense then invites. Starting left of offense and proceeding clockwise, each other player accepts one invitation or declines all, then commits before the next decides. A player may join only one side or neither. Defensive allies place ships beside the target planet, not on it.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 4. Alliance
evidence.text: Offense names invited allies first; they wait to answer. Defense then invites allies, possibly including the same players. Neither main player may invite the other. Starting with the player left of offense and proceeding clockwise, each other player accepts one invitation or declines all, then commits ships before the next player decides. You may join only one side or neither; normally an invitation is required.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > 4. Alliance
evidence.text: Each ally contributes one to four ships from any of their colonies. Offensive allies place them on the gate; defensive allies place them beside the target planet, **not on it**. The FAQ nevertheless considers defensive allies in the gate for effects referring to that location. Parasite changes invitation eligibility.

clauses: Winner for offense attack 10 plus six ships versus defense attack 12 plus four ships.
Destinations of offense, offensive allies, defense, defensive allies, and bystanders.
answers.answer: Both sides total 16 (10 + 6 and 12 + 4), so defense wins the tie. Offense and offensive allies go to the warp; defending and bystander colonies stay; defensive allies return committed ships to any existing own colonies.

evidence.heading: Actions > Attack against attack
evidence.text: Each side's total is its main player's attack value plus all ships on its side: offense and offensive allies in the gate; defense on the target plus defensive allies beside it. Higher total wins; **defense wins ties**. Powers and played cards may change this calculation or the winner.

evidence.heading: Actions > Attack against attack
evidence.text:
- **Offense wins:** all offense and offensive ally ships land on the target, establishing or reinforcing each color's colony. Defense and defensive ally ships go to warp. Bystanders survive. Advance a colony marker only for a newly established foreign colony, not reinforcement of an existing colony.
- **Defense wins:** defending and bystander colonies stay. Offense and offensive allies go to warp. Defensive allies return their committed ships to any existing own colonies, even different origins; helping defend does not grant a colony on the defended planet. Each defensive ally also receives **one defender reward per ship contributed**. For each reward, draw one cosmic-deck card or retrieve one own warp ship to any own colony; combine these choices freely.

clauses: Ship destinations when offense wins an attack.
Whether existing bystander colonies survive.
Whether reinforcing an existing colony earns another colony.
answers.answer: On offense’s win, offense and offensive ally ships land on the target; defense and defensive ally ships go to the warp; bystanders survive. A colony marker advances only for a newly established foreign colony, not reinforcement of an existing colony.

evidence.heading: Actions > Attack against attack
evidence.text:
- **Offense wins:** all offense and offensive ally ships land on the target, establishing or reinforcing each color's colony. Defense and defensive ally ships go to warp. Bystanders survive. Advance a colony marker only for a newly established foreign colony, not reinforcement of an existing colony.
- **Defense wins:** defending and bystander colonies stay. Offense and offensive allies go to warp. Defensive allies return their committed ships to any existing own colonies, even different origins; helping defend does not grant a colony on the defended planet. Each defensive ally also receives **one defender reward per ship contributed**. For each reward, draw one cosmic-deck card or retrieve one own warp ship to any own colony; combine these choices freely.

clauses: Whether a defensive ally contributing three ships may mix card draws and warp retrieval rewards.
Where the ally’s committed ships and retrieved ships go.
answers.answer: Yes. Three contributed ships earn three defender rewards. Each reward may be a cosmic-deck draw or retrieval of one own warp ship, and those choices may be combined freely. The ally’s committed ships return to any existing own colonies; each retrieved ship goes to any own colony.

evidence.heading: Actions > Attack against attack
evidence.text:
- **Offense wins:** all offense and offensive ally ships land on the target, establishing or reinforcing each color's colony. Defense and defensive ally ships go to warp. Bystanders survive. Advance a colony marker only for a newly established foreign colony, not reinforcement of an existing colony.
- **Defense wins:** defending and bystander colonies stay. Offense and offensive allies go to warp. Defensive allies return their committed ships to any existing own colonies, even different origins; helping defend does not grant a colony on the defended planet. Each defensive ally also receives **one defender reward per ship contributed**. For each reward, draw one cosmic-deck card or retrieve one own warp ship to any own colony; combine these choices freely.

clauses: Compensation for the losing main player’s three warp losses, excluding two allied losses.
Source and random/hidden nature of compensation.
Outcome when the opponent has fewer than three cards.
answers.answer: The losing main player takes three cards at random from the opponent’s hand, without seeing their faces; the two allied ships do not count. If the opponent has fewer than three cards, take the entire hand.

evidence.heading: Actions > Attack against negotiate: compensation
evidence.text: The negotiate player automatically loses; resolve the winner's ship destinations normally. The losing main player randomly takes one card from the opponent's hand for each of **their own ships actually lost to the warp**. Exclude allied losses: allies receive no compensation. If the opponent lacks sufficient cards, take the entire hand. Cards are taken without seeing their faces. Compensation is stolen hand cards; defender rewards are deck draws and/or warp retrieval.

clauses: What happens to allies when both main players reveal negotiate.
Permitted exchanges and where a colony can be granted.
Requirements for a valid deal.
Time limit and failure penalty.
answers.answer: Allies return ships to their own colonies, gain nothing, and cannot participate. The main players have one minute to transfer hand cards and/or grant each other one colony on a planet where the giver already has a colony, including a foreign colony. A deal must actually transfer at least one card or colony and may be one-sided; doing nothing is invalid. Tangible terms are limited to permitted cards or colonies and specific power/card exceptions; future promises are unenforceable, and card terms must be truthful and honored. If no agreement is reached in time, each main player loses three ships of their choice to the warp, and offense cannot take an ordinary second encounter.

evidence.heading: Actions > Negotiate against negotiate: making a deal
evidence.text: Both sides' allies return ships to their own colonies, gain nothing and cannot participate in the deal. The main players have **one minute**. They may transfer cards from their hands and/or each grant the other **one colony on a planet where the giver already has a colony**, including a foreign colony. The recipient can use any own ships not in the warp. Existing ships coexist; the giver need not vacate, and vacating would eliminate the colony being offered. Return any remaining gate ships to offense's colonies.

evidence.heading: Actions > Negotiate against negotiate: making a deal
evidence.text: A successful deal must actually transfer at least one card or colony; it may be one-sided. You cannot agree to do nothing. Tangible terms are restricted to permitted cards/colonies and specific power/card exceptions such as Zombie's liberation; future promises are unenforceable. Card terms may be explicit or vague but must be truthful and honored (if you promise your highest attack, give it). If time expires without agreement, **each main player loses three ships of their choice to the warp**, and offense cannot take an ordinary second encounter. Successful deals qualify for an ordinary second encounter but do not trigger win-only powers.

clauses: What Morph copies and when.
Whether Morph tracks later changes to the opponent’s card.
What happens to Morph after the encounter.
answers.answer: Morph becomes an exact copy of the opponent’s initially revealed encounter card (including the attack’s initial value). Later changes to the opponent’s card do not automatically carry over; Morph can be modified separately. After resolution Morph returns to its normal identity and is normally discarded with the other revealed card unless an effect changes its destination.

evidence.heading: Actions > Morph
evidence.text: The single base Morph becomes an exact copy of the opponent's initially revealed encounter card: attack copies its initial value, negotiate becomes negotiate. Resolve that pairing normally. Subsequent modifications of the opponent's card do not automatically carry over to Morph; Morph can be modified separately. For example, Tripler revealing Morph against attack12 copies12 and divides its own copy to4; Tripler revealing12 against Morph changes its own12 to4, while opponent's Morph remains12. After resolution, Morph returns to its normal identity and is normally discarded with the other revealed encounter card, unless an effect changes its destination. If two Morphs could be played against each other, both sides would lose all involved ships to warp; there is only one in this base deck.

clauses: Who may play reinforcements and when.
Which side may receive reinforcements.
When the response window ends.
answers.answer: After encounter cards are revealed during Reveal, either main player and any ally may play reinforcements to either side’s total, including the opposing side. Players may respond with more until all pass; then resolve using the new totals.

evidence.heading: Actions > Artifacts and reinforcements
evidence.text: Reinforcements are not encounter cards. During Reveal, after encounter cards are revealed, either main player and any ally may play them to add to **either side's total**, including the opposing side. Players may respond with further reinforcements until all pass; then resolve using the new totals. Bystanders cannot play them merely because they are present on the planet.

clauses: Ordinary per-player flare limit per encounter.
Per-card flare limit per encounter, including a change of hands.
When a played flare returns to hand.
When an alien uses its own Wild instead of Super.
answers.answer: A player may play at most one flare per encounter, and each flare can be used only once per encounter even if it changes hands. A flare returns to hand immediately after its effect finishes unless its effect says otherwise. Normally use Wild, but if it is your own alien’s flare and your power is available, you must use Super; if the power is lost or zapped, only Wild is available until the power returns.

evidence.heading: Flare system
evidence.text: Flares are not encounter cards. Each has printed Wild and Super effects, usage roles and timing. Normally use Wild; if it is your own alien's flare and your power is available, **you must use Super**, not choose Wild. If your power is lost or zapped, you can use only Wild until your power returns.

evidence.heading: Flare system
evidence.text: Return a flare to hand **immediately after its effect finishes**, rather than discard it, unless its effect states otherwise. A player may play **at most one flare per encounter**, and an individual flare can be used **only once per encounter even if it changes hands**. A Card Zap targeting the flare counts against the player's limit. Prevention of play differs from cancellation after play: see Anti-Matter's FAQ exception. If a Super enables a power use, that power can still be Cosmic Zapped even outside its usual role/phase. The flare remains in hand rather than being discarded or forced to Wild; Wild becomes available while the power is zapped. When your own Wild would otherwise be handed to your alien, keep it after resolution.

clauses: Start-turn replacement when offense lacks encounter cards.
Planning replacement when defense lacks encounter cards.
Later loss of offense’s last encounter card when needed.
Ship returns and whether other cards must be played first.
answers.answer: At Start Turn, offense reveals and discards the remaining hand and draws eight; it may first play legally playable non-encounter cards but is not required to. At Planning, a defense without encounter cards reveals/discards the remainder and draws eight repeatedly until it has one. Later, when offense needs an encounter card and has none, its turn ends rather than replacing the hand; offense returns committed ships to its own colonies and each ally returns committed ships to their own colonies. If no existing colony can receive a required relocation, ships go to the warp.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > Start Turn and hand replacement
evidence.text: Start Turn occurs only before the first encounter of your turn, before Regroup effects. If offense has no encounter cards, reveal and discard the remaining hand, then draw eight new cards. You may first play legally playable non-encounter cards but are not required to play them. Hate draws a needed starting hand before using its power.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure > Start Turn and hand replacement
evidence.text: At Planning, a defense lacking encounter cards reveals/discards the remainder and draws eight cards, repeating until it has an encounter card. An offense that runs out later in its turn **when it needs to play an encounter card** ends its turn instead of drawing a replacement. Offense returns its committed ships to its own colonies; each ally returns that ally's committed ships to that ally's own colonies. The normal no-colony relocation rule applies. There is no automatic draw at the end of an encounter or turn, or merely for running out of cards. Alien and card effects can grant different draws.

evidence.heading: Special Rules & Edge Cases > Colonies, relocation and losses
evidence.text: Removing your last ship from a planet immediately loses that colony. Returning ships must go to **existing** colonies, not abandoned planets; if no colony can receive a required relocation, those ships go to warp unless an explicit exception applies. You still defend an empty home planet with zero ships. Extra ship losses normally let the losing player choose their ships, unless the effect specifies someone else. A requirement to lose ships outside the encounter cannot be paid with encounter ships; if you have no eligible ships, lose none. Likewise you cannot activate a sacrifice requiring an outside ship by substituting an inside ship. Forced losses/sacrifices normally choose ships you control, not ships already in warp, removed or captured.

clauses: Whether offense may start a second encounter without an encounter card in hand, hoping to get one later.
What ends an ordinary turn after the first or second encounter.
answers.answer: No. Offense must already have at least one encounter card in hand to start a second encounter; it cannot start one hoping to obtain a card before Planning. After a second encounter, or an unsuccessful first encounter, the turn passes left. A successful first encounter can qualify for a second; Machine is an exception.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure
evidence.text: The active player is the **offense**. Offense and defense are the **main players**. A turn normally has one encounter and, optionally, a second after a successful first encounter. Winning or making a successful deal is successful; making a deal is **not a win** for an effect that only says win. A second encounter requires at least one encounter card already in the offense's hand; you cannot start it hoping to obtain one before Planning. After the second encounter, or an unsuccessful first encounter, the turn passes left. Machine provides an exception.

clauses: When an ordinary alien power is lost and regained based on home colony count.
Whether it may be used one last time upon loss.
Whether Cosmic Zap stops every printed part of the sheet.
answers.answer: At fewer than three home colonies, the player immediately turns the sheet facedown and loses the power, with no last use; it returns faceup at three or more home planets. Cosmic Zap cancels a cancellable power use and prevents further uses that encounter, but clauses that do not require use are not themselves zappable and remain unaffected.

evidence.heading: Special Rules & Edge Cases > Power loss, zapping and timing
evidence.text: With fewer than **three home colonies**, immediately turn your alien sheet facedown and lose its power; you cannot use it one last time. Restore it faceup when you again occupy at least three home planets. Masochist expressly keeps its power with fewer colonies. Losing a power also removes that alien identity for power-dependent effects and access to its Super.

evidence.heading: Special Rules & Edge Cases > Power loss, zapping and timing
evidence.text: A power may be Cosmic Zapped **only when being used**, not preemptively. The bold-italic **use** on an alien sheet identifies its cancellable use. Cancel that effect and prevent further uses until the encounter ends, including when zapped during Start Turn. Clauses that do not require use—such as Warrior adding experience, Zombie liberating ships in a deal, or placing a Citadel—are not themselves zappable uses. Zapping a use does not disable such clauses.

clauses: Resolution order for truly simultaneous contradictory effects.
Whether another non-Zap action can interrupt a resolving effect.
Whether a power can be Cosmic Zapped preemptively.
answers.answer: Resolve simultaneous contradictory effects in this order: offense, defense, then other players clockwise starting left of offense. Finish one effect before starting another, except a Zap or an effect expressly allowing interruption; once an effect targets a hand and begins resolving, only a Zap or specific interrupt can intervene. A power can be zapped only when being used, not preemptively.

evidence.heading: Special Rules & Edge Cases > Power loss, zapping and timing
evidence.text: Effects associated with no player resolve last, after the player order. Resolve actual simultaneous contradictory effects in order: **offense; defense; other players clockwise starting left of offense**. First honor more specific before/after timing within a phase. Finish one effect before starting another, except a Zap or an effect expressly allowing interruption. An optional effect's owner may change their mind when another effect or timing order changes the game state. Alien powers are normally usable once per relevant context, unless their text says otherwise.

evidence.heading: Special Rules & Edge Cases > Power loss, zapping and timing
evidence.text: Cards may be legally played before compensation starts, but compensation does not permit arbitrary interruptions. Once an effect targets a hand and begins resolving, only a Zap or specific interrupt can intervene. You cannot wait for Hacker to select you and then dump reinforcements: the Reveal window has already passed.

evidence.heading: Special Rules & Edge Cases > Power loss, zapping and timing
evidence.text: A power may be Cosmic Zapped **only when being used**, not preemptively. The bold-italic **use** on an alien sheet identifies its cancellable use. Cancel that effect and prevent further uses until the encounter ends, including when zapped during Start Turn. Clauses that do not require use—such as Warrior adding experience, Zombie liberating ships in a deal, or placing a Citadel—are not themselves zappable uses. Zapping a use does not disable such clauses.

clauses: When ordinary five-foreign-colony victories are checked and whether they can be shared.
Tick-Tock outcome when its last token is removed by a deal that gives both main players their fifth foreign colony.
answers.answer: Ordinary victory is checked at the very end of Resolution; players who simultaneously meet five current foreign colonies share victory. Tick-Tock wins immediately when its last token is removed. When a deal gives both main players their fifth foreign colony while removing Tick-Tock’s last token, all three share the win.

evidence.heading: Scoring / Victory Conditions
evidence.text: Track **current** foreign colonies, decreasing the marker when one is lost. At the **very end of Resolution**, a player with five foreign colonies wins; multiple players meeting the condition together share victory. Other effects still have until that point to prevent ordinary victory. An effect explicitly saying immediately win ends the game when resolved, unless zapped or specifically interrupted. Masochist and Tick-Tock have printed alternate win conditions; Tick-Tock can share a deal-created win as described in its entry.

evidence.heading: Special Rules & Edge Cases > Tick-Tock
evidence.text:
- Setup: Place ten tokens on sheet.
- Each time any player wins as defense OR successful deal made between any two players, discard one token from sheet.
- If no tokens left on sheet immediately win game. May also win normally.
